title: Sidecar Ledger
user: Photographers moving RAW/DNG files between editors and self-hosted libraries who need to know which ratings, descriptions, and edits will survive each handoff.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user reports that Immich's documented read-only-library setup cannot retain tags, descriptions, or ratings because sidecar writes fail and later metadata extraction overwrites them.
A photographer describes a Lightroom-to-Snapseed DNG workflow in which the later editor does not show prior edits.

recurrence: Two independent photo workflows in 2025–2026 expose the same trust failure: state is silently lost or unavailable at a tool boundary; it is severe because it can invalidate hours of editing and curation.
current_workaround: Keep notes manually, duplicate originals, make rendered intermediates, or discover after import that a catalog's sidecar policy was incompatible.
incumbents_and_gap: Lightroom, Immich, darktable, and ExifTool each manage part of the workflow. None is a small, vendor-neutral preflight that states which metadata and edit representations will be portable between two chosen tools.
smallest_useful_product: Local CLI that inventories a folder plus XMP sidecars, compares declared source/destination capabilities, and emits a handoff manifest showing portable, lossy, and unknown fields. Non-goals: image editing, cloud sync, or attempting to reverse-engineer proprietary adjustment recipes.
success_measure: In a 20-photographer pilot, at least 12 use a report before an editor/library migration and at least 8 change their export or backup plan because of a reported loss risk.
monetization: one-time — photographers need an occasional local migration safeguard, not another subscription tied to their private archive.
constraints: Operate locally; do not upload images or EXIF. Treat proprietary edit metadata as opaque, preserve timestamps, and make every suggested write opt-in with a dry run.
why_distinct: The deliverable is an evidence-backed handoff contract, not a replacement photo catalog or a generic metadata editor.

title: Capture Clock Repair
user: Photographers consolidating photos from cameras, phones, messengers, and travel across time zones who need to repair missing or shifted capture times without overwriting trustworthy originals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Nikon user reports that drag-and-drop uploads can shift an image's taken time by one hour after a cross-time-zone edit workflow.
A user with several thousand WhatsApp images asks how to fill DateTimeOriginal only when it is missing, while leaving already valid metadata alone.

recurrence: Two different provenance problems—timezone drift and messenger-stripped timestamps—appear within five months; both make chronological archives unreliable.
current_workaround: Run delicate ExifTool commands, use filesystem time as a proxy, correct files one by one, or accept a wrong timeline.
incumbents_and_gap: ExifTool is powerful but command-oriented; PhotoPrism and catalog apps correct dates after import. The missing layer is a conservative plan/review workflow that distinguishes missing data from conflicting data before any write.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI that groups by camera/source, flags timezone and filename/date conflicts, proposes reversible XMP sidecar patches, and outputs a review CSV. Non-goals: face recognition, cloud photo storage, or claiming forensic certainty.
success_measure: At least 75% of pilot runs accept or amend a proposed correction plan, with zero reported changes to files that already had an accepted DateTimeOriginal value.
monetization: one-time — the value is safe recovery of an existing archive and must work offline.
constraints: Never alter originals by default; preserve timezone offsets; support a complete undo manifest; clearly label inferred dates as inferred.
why_distinct: It makes a reversible decision plan for mixed-source timestamps rather than being another EXIF tag editor.

title: Tempo Earcheck
user: Instrumentalists choosing practice and ensemble tempos who need to hear, tap, and record a defensible target tempo before they encode it in a score or rehearsal plan.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A MuseScore user asks for an audible click in the tempo picker because repeatedly setting a score tempo and reaching for a separate tap-tempo app is tedious.
An accordion player asks for a concrete method to learn melodies and build the ability to play along.

recurrence: Independent composition and practice requests show that tempo choice is made outside the score and then poorly connected to a learning plan; the harm is wasted rehearsal cycles rather than a one-off inconvenience.
current_workaround: Use a separate metronome or tap-tempo app, remember a number informally, then manually re-enter it into notation and practice notes.
incumbents_and_gap: MuseScore, Soundbrenner, and ordinary metronomes play clicks. They do not preserve a small local record of the tempo trial, meter, difficulty note, and next increment for a particular practice target.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with tap-tempo, accented-meter click, named tempo trials, and a compact practice card that records a starting BPM, passed BPM, and next step. Non-goals: streaming music, score hosting, or AI performance grading.
success_measure: At least 50% of weekly active pilots create three or more practice cards and return to one card on a later day to change its tempo based on the recorded result.
monetization: one-time — a musician's personal rehearsal notebook should remain usable without an account.
constraints: Web Audio must work without network access; provide hearing-safe volume defaults; no copyrighted scores or recordings are included.
why_distinct: It links tempo audition to a repeatable rehearsal decision, rather than duplicating a bare metronome.

title: Rehearsal Sightline
user: Orchestra and band players practicing from their own MusicXML scores who need to see what is coming before the playhead reaches it and choose manageable rehearsal slices.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An orchestra user says continuous-mode practice needs a configurable playback margin so players can read the next material while playing.
A guitarist asks how to judge whether a fast solo is beyond their current ability before committing to learning it.

recurrence: One requester needs anticipation during ensemble playback and another needs to scope a difficult passage; both are planning problems around upcoming material, not notation creation.
current_workaround: Scroll a score manually, loop an arbitrary selection, or make handwritten notes about where a passage becomes unplayable.
incumbents_and_gap: MuseScore provides notation and playback, while forScore manages documents. Neither turns user-supplied MusicXML into a deliberately sized rehearsal queue with look-ahead cues and personal pass/fail notes.
smallest_useful_product: Static web app that imports MusicXML locally, lets a player mark rehearsal ranges, renders a configurable look-ahead strip, and exports a printable cue sheet. Non-goals: PDF OCR, score marketplace, collaboration, or copyright-content distribution.
success_measure: In an ensemble pilot, 60% of users complete at least four marked ranges and report fewer unplanned stops in one rehearsal compared with their prior method.
monetization: one-time — local score utilities suit occasional project use and avoid licensing pressure around repertoire.
constraints: Keep imported scores in-browser by default; support only user-provided MusicXML in v1; do not distribute copyrighted notation.
why_distinct: The useful artifact is a player-specific rehearsal plan and sightline, not a general notation editor.

title: Playlist Path Linter
user: Musicians and serious local-library listeners moving playlists between taggers, servers, and devices who need to catch path, Unicode, and date corruption before an import silently drops music.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Beets user reports that an album import writes original-date fields as 0000 when the Deezer plugin is enabled.
A Navidrome user reports that M3U import still skips tracks whose mixed-language paths contain accented characters.

recurrence: Two separate local-music stacks report silent library corruption or omissions during import in July–August 2026; it is high severity because the resulting library looks complete until a set or playlist fails.
current_workaround: Rescan a server, hand-edit M3U files, rename folders, disable plugins, or compare missing tracks manually.
incumbents_and_gap: Beets and Navidrome own their respective imports. No small neutral checker validates an M3U and its library tree across Unicode normalization, relative paths, missing files, and suspicious tag values before handoff.
smallest_useful_product: CLI that reads M3U/M3U8 plus a library root, resolves NFC/NFD variants, reports missing/ambiguous paths and invalid year/date tags, and emits an optional corrected copy plus JSON report. Non-goals: downloading music, metadata lookup, or running a media server.
success_measure: At least 90% of fixture playlists with known missing, normalization, and date defects are diagnosed with a precise file-level explanation; five pilot users fix a real import before it reaches a server.
monetization: free — interoperability utilities benefit from transparent local behavior; paid support is not required for v1.
constraints: Read-only by default; preserve encoding; never contact music services; test paths on case-sensitive and case-insensitive filesystems.
why_distinct: It checks the boundary between music-library tools instead of proposing another tagger or streaming library.

title: Route Fidelity Check
user: Cyclists who plan a GPX route in one service and ride it on another device who need proof that the transferred route still follows the intended trail and has no discontinuities.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A BRouter user documents rare unexplained gaps in calculated routes despite the underlying OSM data appearing continuous.
A rider's RideWithGPS rail-trail route is replaced by nearby roads after Garmin transfer even though Garmin's site displays the trail.

recurrence: These independent route-engine and device-transfer failures span a year; the consequence is a route that is unsafe or unusable only after leaving home.
current_workaround: Visually inspect on a device, compare map screenshots, add many waypoints, or hope a navigation app does not recalculate.
incumbents_and_gap: RideWithGPS, Garmin Connect, Komoot, and BRouter plan or navigate routes. They do not offer a service-neutral before/after GPX comparison focused on snapped-away trail segments, gaps, and changed distance.
smallest_useful_product: Static web tool that compares an intended and exported GPX locally, flags discontinuities and segments farther than a user-set tolerance, and renders a shareable pre-ride checklist. Non-goals: routing, turn-by-turn navigation, or map-data editing.
success_measure: On a corpus of 30 altered GPX pairs, it flags 95% of intentional gaps or >50 m diversions; at least 10 pilot riders run it before a ride in the first month.
monetization: free — local GPX comparison is a trust-building utility with low operating cost.
constraints: Process GPX in-browser; warn that geometric agreement is not a safety assessment; use an open map tile provider only if the user opts in.
why_distinct: It validates transfer fidelity between existing route products rather than competing to plan the route.

title: Bike Service Timeline
user: Owners of multiple bicycles who need a complete, portable component-service history and a clear next-service view across every bike.

evidence.quote_or_summary: VeloGarage explicitly requests a full cross-bike maintenance log because its bike detail only shows recent entries for one bike.
A long-time rider asks for a dependable brake-pad installation technique after repeatedly struggling with a small maintenance task for decades.

recurrence: The tools-side request and a hands-on repair question show that maintenance knowledge is both fragmented and episodic; a missed history matters when parts wear differently across bikes.
current_workaround: Keep paper notes, rely on recent activity in one bike app, search chat history, or remember when a part was last touched.
incumbents_and_gap: ProBikeGarage, VeloGarage, and ride logs track intervals, but cross-bike history and a durable, exportable maintenance narrative are not consistently first-class. A simple ownership record remains underserved.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with bikes, components, service entries, receipts/photos, mileage/date triggers, and one chronological all-bike view exportable as CSV/print. Non-goals: parts marketplace, mechanic booking, or diagnostic advice.
success_measure: At least 70% of pilot owners with two or more bikes log five service entries and can answer when a named component was last serviced without searching another app.
monetization: one-time — the service record should remain available even if the rider stops paying.
constraints: Local-first with explicit export/backup; retain only user-entered records; interval guidance must be configurable and never represented as safety certification.
why_distinct: It is a portable ownership timeline across bikes, not a ride tracker or a generic to-do list.

title: Nightjar Slicer
user: Birders recording long overnight AudioMoth or field-recorder files who need to split, sample, and queue clips for BirdNET analysis without crashing a GUI or waiting through repeated extraction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A BirdNET Analyzer user reports clip extraction for training becoming roughly 40 times slower after a processing-path change.
A user reports BirdNET-GUI disappearing when a 4 GB overnight AudioMoth recording is opened.

recurrence: Two BirdNET Analyzer users report different long-recording bottlenecks within three weeks: one cannot open a 4 GB file and another finds clip preparation dramatically slower.
current_workaround: Manually split WAV files, wait for a full analysis, reduce recordings arbitrarily, or abandon a recording after the GUI fails.
incumbents_and_gap: BirdNET Analyzer identifies birds and Audacity splits audio, but neither makes a low-risk analysis queue from a large field recording with inspectable time ranges and resumable chunks.
smallest_useful_product: Local CLI that reads WAV/FLAC headers, makes fixed or silence-aware chunks, emits a timestamped manifest and spectrogram thumbnails, and can resume a failed batch. Non-goals: species identification model, cloud upload, or automatic public reporting.
success_measure: On 4 GB reference recordings, it creates a resume-safe manifest without exceeding a 1 GB memory ceiling and enables 10 pilot users to submit at least one selected chunk to their existing analyzer.
monetization: free — transparent local preprocessing is most useful as a companion to existing open bird-analysis tools.
constraints: Do not bundle BirdNET weights or claim identification accuracy; preserve original recordings; make sensitive-location metadata removal the default in exported manifests.
why_distinct: It solves the recording-scale handoff before identification, not another bird-recognition wrapper.

title: Field Evidence Notes
user: Birders making uncertain observations of feathers, behavior, or remains who need a private, structured evidence record before asking an expert or submitting a sensitive sighting.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user trying to identify a feather reports that Google Lens provided no close visual match and an AI summary made an uncertain owl claim.
A birder describes a puzzling grackle behavior in detail and asks whether it is courtship, tool use, or play.

recurrence: Two independent observers need to preserve context for an uncertain field observation: one for physical evidence and one for behavior. The need is recurring at the moment an observation is made, when details decay quickly.
current_workaround: Put loose photos and notes in a phone album, post an underspecified question, or rely on an AI image guess without a record of uncertainty and context.
incumbents_and_gap: eBird and iNaturalist are excellent public observation systems, but their submission flows are not designed as a private uncertainty-first notebook for evidence that may not be appropriate to publish or identify yet.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA for time, coarse location, measurements, photos, field marks, behavior, and confidence; export a concise expert-question packet with coordinates redacted by default. Non-goals: automated species ID, social feed, or public rarity alerts.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot observations export a complete evidence packet with date, location precision, and two or more field-mark fields; no export includes exact coordinates unless explicitly enabled.
monetization: free — privacy-preserving field notes need trust and have negligible server cost.
constraints: Local-first; obscure sensitive species and nest locations by default; include a clear warning that an evidence packet is not an identification or wildlife-handling instruction.
why_distinct: It captures the evidence and uncertainty before an ID claim, rather than competing as another automated bird identifier.

title: Shelf Bridge
user: Board-game collectors moving a BoardGameGeek collection into a personal tracker who need their ownership, wishlist, and past-ownership states to survive an import predictably.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Yamtrack user asks for a BoardGameGeek collection importer and explicitly proposes mappings for wishlist and previously owned games.
A board-game lover requests a dedicated NeoDB board-game category to mark, comment on, and browse board games, citing existing collection apps and databases.

recurrence: Two independent tracker communities request first-class board-game collection handling across 2025–2026; status and personal annotation are the missing details, not merely title lookup.
current_workaround: Export BGG CSV, import only the rows a target accepts, then recreate statuses and notes by hand or keep multiple trackers in parallel.
incumbents_and_gap: BoardGameGeek, BG Stats, Yamtrack, and NeoDB maintain collections or play logs. Their import conventions are different, leaving collectors without a transparent mapping and review step between systems.
smallest_useful_product: Static web converter that imports a BGG collection export, lets users map statuses/ratings/comments to a target-neutral schema, validates duplicates, and exports CSV/JSON profiles for Yamtrack and NeoDB-style imports. Non-goals: scraping BGG, hosting a collection, price tracking, or copying game art.
success_measure: At least 80% of ten real BGG exports complete a conversion with zero unreviewed status drops; half of pilot users export to two destinations from the same normalized file.
monetization: free — a transparent client-side converter earns trust and is a narrow interoperability utility.
constraints: Use only user-supplied exports; respect BGG and target-service terms; do not redistribute game metadata, images, or reviews; process files locally.
why_distinct: It is a reviewable collection-state bridge, not a replacement BGG database or another play-log app.

title: Limited Night Planner
user: Hosts running a casual limited card or tabletop event from a mixed personal collection who need to turn uncertain inventory into a fair, timed, low-friction night.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A host with more than 2,000 bulk cards asks for a fun limited event so friends can build decks and take cards home instead of merely storing or selling them.
A player asks whether a replacement card deck differs from the base Ticket to Ride deck beyond six locomotives, illustrating the component-compatibility uncertainty hosts face.

recurrence: Both 2025 questions arise when a host must make a playable event from physical components whose composition or compatibility is uncertain; bad setup wastes the whole group's session.
current_workaround: Use a spreadsheet, count components by hand, search rules/forums, and improvise seating, rounds, and timers during the event.
incumbents_and_gap: Challonge handles brackets and publisher apps handle specific games. There is no lightweight, rules-neutral planner that starts with a host's component counts and emits a setup, rounds, and exception checklist without needing a proprietary card database.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with inventory counts, player count, pack/pool assumptions, round timer, seating rotation, and printable host sheet; users write their own compatibility notes. Non-goals: official rules text, card database, matchmaking, or online play.
success_measure: In 15 hosted events, at least 12 begin within ten minutes of the planned start and hosts use the generated checklist for every round transition.
monetization: one-time — hosts value a dependable event tool that works in venues with poor connectivity.
constraints: No copyrighted rules or card images; all game-specific content is user-entered; support printing and local export.
why_distinct: It plans the physical event from uncertain inventory; it is not another rules wiki, bracket site, or virtual tabletop.

title: Water & Rig Notebook
user: Anglers recording water conditions and planning line or trotline rigs who need a private, repeatable way to relate a catch/rig log to depth, current, buoyancy, and local constraints.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A hobby-app roadmap explicitly identifies a fly-fishing hatch chart and water-condition log as a standalone enthusiast-tool need.
An angler planning a 100 m freshwater trotline with 19 snoods asks how much anchoring weight is needed under site-specific conditions.

recurrence: The 2025 practical rig question and 2026 hatch/water-log proposal point to the same missing personal record: conditions and setup are inseparable, yet are usually kept in memory or separate tools.
current_workaround: Use a notes app, screenshots of forecasts, generic fishing apps, forum advice, and mental estimates for line/weight decisions.
incumbents_and_gap: Fishbrain and local forecast apps emphasize discovery and social reports; generic fishing logs do not pair a transparent personal conditions record with a conservative rig worksheet that remains private and exportable.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with per-waterbody condition entries, rig templates, catch/outcome notes, and a clearly labeled line/anchor worksheet using user-entered depth/current/buoyancy assumptions. Non-goals: live fish maps, fishing forecasts, social feed, or legal/safety advice.
success_measure: At least 10 pilot anglers log three outings each and can retrieve a prior rig/condition combination before a repeat trip; all worksheet exports show the assumptions used.
monetization: one-time — a private field notebook should function offline without a recurring data fee.
constraints: No automatic location sharing; calculations must show inputs and uncertainty, never certify a safe anchor or legal method; local regulations and species rules remain the user's responsibility.
why_distinct: It is a private conditions-to-rig learning record with an explainable worksheet, not a social fishing map or forecast clone.
